back: The continuous movement of an element (such as carbon or nitrogen) between living things, rocks and soil, and the air and water.

front: The three stores and three transfers of the nutrient cycle
back: Stores: biomass, litter, soil. Transfers: fallout (biomass → litter), decomposition (litter → soil), uptake (soil → biomass).

front: Inputs and outputs of the nutrient cycle
back: Inputs: weathering of rock, nutrients in rain and dust. Outputs: leaching, runoff and erosion, harvesting.

front: Largest nutrient store in a tropical rainforest
back: Biomass: litter rots fast, roots take nutrients up quickly and heavy rain leaches the soil.
Changing nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use, by bacteria in legume root nodules, lightning or fertiliser factories.
Nitrification: bacteria turn ammonium into nitrates. Denitrification: bacteria turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas, mainly in waterlogged soil.

front: Processes that return carbon dioxide to the air
back: Respiration, decomposition and combustion (burning wood, charcoal, fossil fuels, veld fires).
Excess nutrients (from fertiliser or sewage) cause rapid algal growth; decay of the algae uses up oxygen and fish die.
The washing of dissolved nutrients down through the soil, out of reach of roots, by heavy rain.
